links.passage: When testing the performance of satellite-based ET irrigation controllers, Devitt et al. (2008) found that 81% of ET-based controllers (scheduled automatically according to ET data) achieved water saving when the controllers were individually programmed at each site according to the manufacturer’s recommendations.
reference_entries: Devitt, D., K. Carstensen, and R. Morris. 2008. “Residential water savings associated with satellite-based ET irrigation controllers.” J. Irrig. Drain. Eng. 134 (1): 74–82. https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9437(2008)134:1(74).

links.passage: Davis et al. (2009) showed that when maintaining turfgrass quality an ET-based IS method significantly reduced irrigation water use.

links.passage: Similarly, in Irrigator Pro for cotton irrigation, once the first cracked boll stage occurred, irrigation was applied to return the soil to its maximum AWCðprobeÞ , and then no more irrigation was applied for the rest of the season, promoting boll opening and preventing boll rot and attending yield and quality loss (USDA-ARS, National Peanut Research Laboratory 2019a).
supporting_passages: Developed by the United States Department of Agriculture Agricultural Research Service (USDA-ARS) and University of Georgia on the basis of 25 years of data on conservation-minded irrigation management (USDA-ARS 2016), Irrigator Pro is an expert system designed to provide irrigation scheduling recommendations based on soil measurements like soil ψm and soil temperature.
links.inference_note: The earlier passage identifies Irrigator Pro as a decision-support expert system for irrigation scheduling, and the claim passage states that its scheduling rule promotes boll opening and prevents yield and quality loss.
reference_entries: USDA-ARS (Agriculture Research Service), National Peanut Research Laboratory. 2019a. “Available water content calculation.” Accessed August 23, 2019. https://irrigatorpro.org/#/calculations.

links.passage: A study carried out at the University of Georgia’s Stripling Irrigation Research Park near Camilla, Georgia, by Vellidis et al. (2016b) compared the effectiveness of different cotton IS methods among themselves [Checkbook, SmartIrrigation App and the University of Georgia Smart Sensor Array (UGA-SSA; Vellidis et al. 2013)] and to a strictly rainfed treatment. They found that in a wet year the scheduling methods resulted in a significantly lower yield and water use efficiency than the rainfed treatment.

Robertson. 2016b. “Irrigation scheduling for cotton using soil moisture sensors, smartphone apps, and traditional methods.” In Vol. 16779 of Proc., 2016 Beltwide Cotton Conf., 772–780. (2009) found that a high setting of saturation allowance for the Rain Bird ET Manager controller, that allows for rainfall to be stored in the root zone by not irrigating fully to field capacity, resulted in low soil-water content during periods of low rainfall and therefore affected turf quality.
reference_entries: McCready, M., M. Dukes, and G. Miller. 2009. “Water conservation potential of smart irrigation controllers on St. Augustinegrass.” Agric. Water Manage. 96 (11): 1623–1632. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2009.06.007.

links.passage: A method using soil ψm thresholds decreased applied water but caused severe water stress and decreased fruit quality.
supporting_passages: Osroosh et al. (2016) compared seven different irrigation methods for apple orchards (e.g., ET-WB-based, conventional, Θ-based methods, and plant-based methods) based on the total irrigation water applied, simplicity, and expense for a grower to implement.
Related to Θ, soil water tension or soil matric potential (ψm ), measured by tensiometers, is another parameter used to quantify soil water available for plant use.
links.inference_note: The claim sentence reports a result of the Osroosh et al. (2016) comparison cited two sentences earlier, and the paper elsewhere states that soil ψm is measured by tensiometers, so the ψm-threshold method is a soil-sensor-based schedule that decreased applied water.
reference_entries: Osroosh, Y., R. T. Peters, C. S. Campbell, and Q. Zhang. 2016. “Comparison of irrigation automation algorithms for drip-irrigated apple trees.” Comput. Electron. Agric. 128 (Oct): 87–99. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compag.2016.08.013.
